extraction.name: CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100
extraction.description: Labeled subsets of the 80 million tiny images dataset. CIFAR-10 contains 6000 examples of each of 10 classes (airplane, automobile, bird, cat, deer, dog, frog, horse, ship, truck). CIFAR-100 contains 600 examples of each of 100 non-overlapping classes, organized into 20 superclasses of 5 classes each. Images are 32x32 color images. The datasets were created to provide reliable labels for object recognition experiments, since the original tiny images dataset had unreliable search-term-based labels.
extraction.creator: Alex Krizhevsky (with substantial contribution from Vinod Nair for labeling)
extraction.citeAs: Krizhevsky, A. (2009). Learning Multiple Layers of Features from Tiny Images.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets were created as labeled subsets of the 80 million tiny images dataset. Paid student labelers were given a class and asked to examine all images found with that class as the search term, as well as images found with hyponyms (as defined by WordNet) of the main search term. Labelers filtered out mislabeled images according to specific criteria. Every label submitted by labelers was personally verified by the author. Duplicate images were removed by comparing images with the L2 norm using a liberal rejection threshold. The dataset was then divided into training and test sets, with the training set receiving a randomly-selected 5000 images from each class (for CIFAR-10).
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping, Secondary Data analysis
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The 80 million tiny images dataset collected by colleagues at MIT and NYU, who assembled it by searching the web for images of every non-abstract English noun in the WordNet lexical database. They used several search engines including Google, Flickr, and Altavista, keeping roughly the first 3000 results for each search term. After collecting, they removed perfect duplicates and images with excessively large portions of white pixels (synthetic figures). The dataset contains 80 million color images downscaled to 32x32 and spread across 79000 search terms.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: The original tiny images dataset was collected over the span of six months (as reported in [14]).
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images were downscaled to 32x32 resolution. Perfect duplicates and images with excessively large white regions were removed from the raw tiny images dataset. For the labeled subsets, duplicate images were removed by comparing images with the L2 norm using a liberal rejection threshold to capture not just perfect duplicates but also re-saved JPEGs. For some experiments, ZCA whitening transformation was applied, and the 1000 least significant principal components were deleted.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Labelers were given a class and asked to examine all images found with that class as the search term, as well as images found with hyponyms of the main search term. Criteria for accepting an image: (1) The class name should be high on the list of likely answers to 'What is in this picture?' (2) The image should be photo-realistic (line drawings rejected). (3) The image should contain only one prominent instance of the object. (4) The object may be partially occluded or seen from an unusual viewpoint as long as its identity is still clear. Labelers were instructed that false positives are worse than false negatives. Every label was personally verified by the author.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Every label submitted by the labelers was personally verified by the author.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Paid students. The labelers were paid a fixed sum per hour spent labeling, so there was no incentive to rush through the task.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: CIFAR-100 contains a 'people' superclass with classes: baby, boy, girl, man, woman. These represent human subject categories in the images.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The original search terms used to find images provide rough labels that are extremely unreliable due to the nature of online image search technology. Images tend to be symmetric about the vertical and horizontal axes, probably caused by the way people take photographs—making the ground plane horizontal and centering on the main object.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The original tiny images dataset has no reliable class labels, which makes it hard to use for object recognition experiments—this motivated the creation of CIFAR-10/100. Images are low resolution (32x32). The author noted CIFAR-10 classes have confusion between similar classes (e.g., cats frequently mistaken for dogs).
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, and Validation for object recognition/classification experiments. Used to demonstrate that object recognition is significantly improved by pre-training a layer of features on a large set of unlabeled tiny images. CIFAR-100 classes are mutually exclusive with CIFAR-10 classes, so CIFAR-100 can be used as negative examples for CIFAR-10.
